Thus, the distinction is to be made in this way: whenever we say that the <term>People</term> or the <term>multitude</term> wills, hopes, or acts, we mean the <term>State</term> <gloss>civitas</gloss>, which commands, wills, and acts through the will of <term>one man</term>, or through the concurring wills of <term>many men</term>, which cannot happen except in an <term>assembly</term> <gloss>conventu</gloss>. However, whenever something is said to be done by a multitude of men, whether large or small, without the will of that man or assembly, it is understood to be done by the <term>subject people</term> <note>the body of individuals who are ruled</note>, that is, by many individual citizens together. This does not proceed from a single will, but from the various wills of many different men; these men, being now citizens and subjects, are not the <term>State</term>.

<margin>
The beginning of the state is the right of the greater number consenting.
</margin>

II. Next, it must be considered that every individual from the multitude (so that a beginning for establishing the state may be made) must agree with the others that in those matters proposed by anyone in the gathering, that which the <term>majority</term> <gloss>major pars</gloss> of them wants shall be held as the will of everyone. For otherwise, a multitude of men, whose dispositions and desires differ so widely among themselves, will have no collective will at all. But if anyone is unwilling to agree, the others will nonetheless co<unclear>n</unclear>stitute the state among themselves.

<note>Vocabulary: People, multitude, state, assembly, subjects, will, majority, consensus.</note>

<summary>Hobbes distinguishes between a unified "People," which acts as a single State through a representative or assembly, and a "multitude" of individuals. He establishes that a political body is formed when individuals agree to abide by the will of the majority.</summary>
<keywords>social contract, majority rule, sovereign will, state formation, citizenship, Thomas Hobbes, political theory</keywords>
